items.stem: No atoms are gained or lost in a chemical reaction, yet the mass of product collected is almost always less than the calculated amount. What does this shortfall show?

options.text: A few of the atoms are destroyed as the old bonds are broken apart.
Mass is conserved only when a reaction is done in a sealed flask.
The atoms all still exist, but they are not all in the product.
The balanced equation overstates how much product could form.

items.why: Correct: no atoms are gained or lost, so the missing mass is unreacted material, product lost on separation, or atoms built into a different product.

items.stem: A product is made using a reaction that is reversible. Why does this keep the yield below the maximum theoretical amount?

options.text: The reaction does not go to completion, so some reactant is left over.
All of the product turns back into the reactants, and none is left.
Atoms are used up by the backward reaction and cannot be got back.
The backward reaction uses up the catalyst, so the reaction ends.

items.why: Correct: product re-forms reactant as fast as reactant forms product, so the mixture always still contains some reactant.

items.stem: Copper sulfate crystals are filtered from the reaction mixture, washed and dried before being weighed. Which reason for a low yield does this practical show?

options.text: Filtering strips atoms out of the compound, so it now weighs less.
Water driven off during drying shows mass is not conserved.
Washing adds impurities to the crystals and lowers the mass.
Some product stays on the filter paper and inside the glassware.

items.why: Correct: product lost when it is separated from the reaction mixture is never weighed, so the yield falls below the maximum.

items.stem: A student analyses the product mixture and finds an unexpected second compound in it. Which reason for the reduced yield does this point to?

options.text: The reaction is reversible, so some product has changed back again.
Some reactant reacted in a way different to the expected one.
Filtering and washing took some atoms out of the product itself.
The relative formula masses used in the calculation were wrong.

items.why: Correct: a compound that does not appear in the equation shows that some of the reactants took a different reaction pathway.

items.stem: What does the percentage yield of a reaction tell you?

options.text: The percentage of the product that has not turned back into reactants.
The mass of product made, as a percentage of the maximum theoretical mass.
The mass of product made, as a percentage of the mass of the reactants.
The percentage of reactant atoms ending up in the useful product.

items.why: Correct: the amount of product obtained is the yield, and comparing it with the maximum theoretical amount as a percentage gives the percentage yield.

items.stem: Which calculation gives the percentage yield of a product?

options.text: (maximum theoretical mass of product / mass of the product made) x 100
(mass of product actually made / total mass of all reactants) x 100
(Mr of the desired product / sum of Mr of all reactants) x 100
(mass of product actually made / maximum theoretical mass) x 100

items.why: Correct: the specification formula is % Yield = (Mass of product actually made) / (Maximum theoretical mass of product) x 100.

items.stem: 6.0 g of magnesium is burned in air. The maximum theoretical mass of magnesium oxide is 10.0 g. The student collects 8.5 g of magnesium oxide. What is the percentage yield?
The maximum theoretical mass of a product is 60 g. A student separates and dries the product and obtains 54 g of it. What is the percentage yield?
Calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. Mr: CaCO3 = 100, CaO = 56, CO2 = 44. What is the maximum theoretical mass of calcium oxide that can be made from 10 g of calcium carbonate?

options.text: 4 g

items.why: Correct: 10 / 100 = 0.1 mol of CaCO3, which gives 0.1 mol of CaO, so the mass is 0.1 x 56 = 5.6 g.

items.stem: Iron is extracted in the blast furnace: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2. Mr: Fe2O3 = 160, Fe = 56. What is the maximum theoretical mass of iron that can be made from 20 g of iron(III) oxide?

options.text: 7 g

items.why: Correct: 20 / 160 = 0.125 mol of Fe2O3, and the 2 in 2Fe gives 0.25 mol of Fe, so the mass is 0.25 x 56 = 14 g.

items.stem: What does the atom economy of a reaction measure?

options.text: The amount of the starting materials that ends up as useful product.
The amount of the predicted product that is collected in practice.
The amount of reactant that has reacted once equilibrium has been set up.
The amount of the energy given out that is transferred usefully.

items.why: Correct: atom economy, or atom utilisation, is a measure of the amount of starting materials that end up as useful products.

items.stem: A student weighs out the reactants, weighs the product she has made and divides one measured mass by the other to find the atom economy. Why is this wrong?

options.text: The mass lost when the product was separated must be subtracted.
The atom economy changes when the reaction is scaled up to industry.
The percentage atom economy is calculated using the balanced equation.
The actual yield of product is needed as well as the theoretical.

items.why: Correct: the specification calculates atom economy from relative formula masses in the balanced equation, so measured masses are never used.

items.stem: In the percentage atom economy calculation, what is the bottom line of the fraction?

options.text: The relative formula mass of the desired product from the equation.
The sum of the relative formula masses of all reactants in the equation.
The relative formula mass of the one reactant that the product comes from.
The total mass of all the reactants weighed out in the experiment.

items.why: Correct: the Mr of the desired product is divided by the sum of the relative formula masses of all reactants from the equation.

items.stem: Hydrogen is made from methane: CH4 + H2O -> 3H2 + CO. Mr: CH4 = 16, H2O = 18, H2 = 2, CO = 28. What is the percentage atom economy for making hydrogen?
Titanium is extracted by the reaction TiCl4 + 4Na -> Ti + 4NaCl. Mr: TiCl4 = 190, Na = 23, Ti = 48, NaCl = 58.5. What is the percentage atom economy for titanium?

Two routes make the same product. Route 1: atom economy 42 %, percentage yield 95 %, fast, by-product is waste that must be disposed of. Route 2: atom economy 88 %, percentage yield 90 %, slightly slower, by-product is sold as a fertiliser. Which judgement is best supported by the data?

options.text: Route 1, because its higher percentage yield means that less is wasted.
Route 1, because a faster rate always makes the process a cheaper one.
Route 2, because a high atom economy always gives a high percentage yield.
Route 2, because much more of the reactant mass ends up as product.

items.why: Correct: 88 % atom economy with a 90 % yield and a saleable by-product wastes far less raw material, for the cost of a slightly slower rate.

items.stem: Give one reason why it is important for a company to use a reaction with a high atom economy.

options.text: More of the product predicted by the equation is collected each time.
Less of the starting material is wasted, so raw materials cost less.
The reaction runs faster, so more product is made in the same time.
No by-products are made at all, so there is no waste to deal with.

items.why: Correct: more of the starting material ends up as useful product, which matters for sustainable development, because raw materials are limited, and for economic reasons.

items.stem: A bottle of dilute hydrochloric acid is labelled 0.500 mol/dm³. What does this label tell you about the solution inside?

options.text: Every 1 dm³ of this solution contains 0.500 g of hydrogen chloride.
Every 1 cm³ of this solution holds 0.500 mol of hydrogen chloride.
Every 1 dm³ of this solution contains 0.500 mol of hydrogen chloride.
0.500 mol of hydrogen chloride was stirred into 1 dm³ of water.

items.why: A concentration in mol/dm³ states the amount of solute, in moles, present in each 1 dm³ of solution.

items.stem: Solution P contains 0.0400 mol of potassium hydroxide in 200 cm³ of solution. Solution Q contains 0.0400 mol of potassium hydroxide in 500 cm³ of solution. Which statement about their concentrations in mol/dm³ is correct?

options.text: P is the more concentrated, as the same amount of solute sits in less solution.
Q is the more concentrated, because it contains the larger volume of solution overall.
P and Q are equally concentrated, since each of them holds 0.0400 mol of solute.
Neither concentration can be found until the volume of water used is known.

items.why: Concentration is amount of solute divided by volume of solution, giving 0.200 mol/dm³ for P and 0.0800 mol/dm³ for Q.

items.stem: What amount, in moles, of sodium hydroxide is present in 250 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution of concentration 0.200 mol/dm³?

options.text: 50.0 mol
0.8 mol

items.why: amount in moles = concentration × volume in dm³ = 0.200 × 0.250 = 0.0500 mol.

items.stem: What mass of sodium hydroxide is dissolved in 200 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution of concentration 0.250 mol/dm³? (Relative formula mass of NaOH = 40)
items.why: amount in moles = 0.250 × 0.200 = 0.0500 mol, then mass = 0.0500 × 40 = 2.0 g.

items.stem: In a titration, 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution was neutralised by exactly 20.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.100 mol/dm³. NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O. What is the concentration of the sodium hydroxide solution?

options.text: 0.0800 mol/dm³
0.00200 mol/dm³
0.125 mol/dm³
12.5 mol/dm³

items.stem: In a titration, 20.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution was neutralised by exactly 25.0 cm³ of sulfuric acid of concentration 0.0500 mol/dm³. H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. What is the concentration of the sodium hydroxide solution?

options.text: 0.000125 mol/dm³
0.00250 mol/dm³
0.125 mol/dm³
0.0625 mol/dm³

items.stem: 4.0 g of sodium hydroxide is dissolved in water and the solution is made up to 250 cm³. What is the concentration of the solution in mol/dm³? (Relative formula mass of NaOH = 40)

options.text: 0.00040 mol/dm³
0.400 mol/dm³
0.0250 mol/dm³
16.0 mol/dm³

items.why: amount in moles = 4.0 ÷ 40 = 0.100 mol, then concentration = 0.100 ÷ 0.250 = 0.400 mol/dm³.

items.stem: A student adds 250 cm³ of water to 250 cm³ of sodium chloride solution of concentration 0.800 mol/dm³ and stirs. What happens to the concentration, and why?

options.text: It stays at 0.800 mol/dm³, because no sodium chloride has been added to it or taken from it.
It doubles to 1.60 mol/dm³, because the volume of the solution has been doubled.
It cannot be worked out unless the mass in grams of dissolved solute is given.
It halves to 0.400 mol/dm³, because the same amount of solute is now in twice the volume.

items.why: The amount of sodium chloride is unchanged while the volume of solution doubles, and concentration is amount divided by volume.

items.stem: A sealed flask contains 4.0 g of helium gas, He (Ar = 4). Which sample of methane gas, CH4 (Mr = 16), occupies the same volume under the same conditions of temperature and pressure?

options.text: 16 g of methane gas, CH4
0.25 g of methane, CH4
4.0 g of methane, CH4
64 g of methane, CH4

items.why: 4.0 g of helium is 1 mol and 16 g of CH4 is 1 mol. Equal amounts in moles of gases occupy the same volume under the same conditions of temperature and pressure.

items.stem: Two gas syringes are held at the same temperature and pressure. One contains 0.50 mol of nitrogen, N2 (Mr = 28), and the other contains 0.50 mol of sulfur dioxide, SO2 (Mr = 64). Which statement about the two gas volumes is correct?

options.text: The sulfur dioxide has the larger volume, as its molecules are heavier.
The two volumes are the same, because the amounts in moles are equal.
The nitrogen has the smaller volume, as it is the lighter gas here.
The volumes cannot be compared, as the two masses are different.

items.why: Equal amounts in moles of gases occupy the same volume under the same conditions of temperature and pressure, whatever the gas.

items.stem: What is the volume of one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure (20 °C and 1 atmosphere pressure)?

options.text: 22.4 dm³ for each mole
24 cm³ for every mole
24 dm³ for each mole
2.4 dm³ for a mole

items.why: The specification states that the volume of one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure (20 °C and 1 atmosphere pressure) is 24 dm³.

items.stem: A balloon holds 3.0 mol of argon gas at room temperature and pressure. What is the volume of the gas in the balloon?

options.text: 24 dm³ of argon gas
67.2 dm³ of argon
8.0 dm³ of argon
72 dm³ of argon

items.why: One mole occupies 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure, so volume = 3.0 × 24 = 72 dm³.

items.stem: A sample of carbon dioxide gas, CO2 (Mr = 44), has a mass of 8.8 g. What is the volume of this sample at room temperature and pressure?

options.text: 211.2 dm³ of carbon dioxide
4.8 dm³ of carbon dioxide gas
0.37 dm³ of carbon dioxide
120 dm³ of carbon dioxide

items.why: Amount = 8.8 ÷ 44 = 0.2 mol, and volume = 0.2 × 24 = 4.8 dm³ at room temperature and pressure.

items.stem: What is the volume of 4.0 g of oxygen gas, O2, at room temperature and pressure? (Ar of O = 16)

options.text: 6.0 dm³ of the gas
96 dm³ of oxygen
0.17 dm³ of gas
3.0 dm³ of oxygen

items.why: Mr(O2) = 32, so amount = 4.0 ÷ 32 = 0.125 mol and volume = 0.125 × 24 = 3.0 dm³.

items.stem: At room temperature and pressure, volume (dm³) = amount of substance (mol) × 24. A student has measured the volume of a gas in dm³ and wants the amount in moles. Which step gives the amount in moles?

options.text: Subtract 24 from the volume in dm³.
Multiply the volume in dm³ by 24.
Divide the volume in dm³ by 24.
Divide 24 by the gas volume.

items.why: The 24 multiplies the amount, so dividing both sides by 24 makes the amount the subject: amount = volume ÷ 24.

items.stem: For a gas at room temperature and pressure, volume (dm³) = (mass (g) ÷ Mr) × 24. A student knows the volume and the Mr of the gas and wants its mass. Which pair of steps gives the mass?

options.text: Multiply the volume by the Mr, and then divide by 24.
Multiply the volume by 24, then divide by the Mr.
Divide the volume by the Mr, then divide by 24.
Divide the volume by 24 and then by the Mr.

items.why: Undoing one step at a time gives mass = volume × Mr ÷ 24: the Mr was dividing so it now multiplies, and the 24 was multiplying so it now divides.

items.stem: Calcium carbonate decomposes on heating: CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g). A student wants to use this equation to work out gas volumes at room temperature and pressure. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Only the carbon dioxide has a gas volume here.
Every substance shown occupies 24 dm³ per mole.
The calcium oxide also occupies 24 dm³ per mole.
The calcium carbonate also occupies 24 dm³ per mole.

items.why: The molar gas volume of 24 dm³ applies to gases only, and the state symbols show that carbon dioxide is the one gas in this equation.

items.stem: Nitrogen reacts with hydrogen: N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g). 30 cm³ of nitrogen reacts completely with excess hydrogen. What volume of ammonia is formed, measured at the same temperature and pressure?

options.text: 1.25 cm³ of ammonia gas
60 cm³ of ammonia, NH3
30 cm³ of ammonia gas
90 cm³ of NH3 formed

items.why: The gases are at the same conditions, so the balancing numbers give the volume ratio directly: N2 : NH3 is 1 : 2, so 30 × 2 = 60 cm³.

items.stem: Carbon monoxide burns in oxygen: 2CO(g) + O2(g) → 2CO2(g). What volume of oxygen reacts completely with 100 cm³ of carbon monoxide, both gases measured at the same temperature and pressure?

options.text: 200 cm³ of oxygen needed
4.2 cm³ of O2 needed
50 cm³ of oxygen used
100 cm³ of oxygen used

items.why: At the same temperature and pressure the balancing numbers give the volume ratio: CO : O2 is 2 : 1, so 100 ÷ 2 = 50 cm³.

items.stem: Ethene burns completely: C2H4(g) + 3O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 2H2O(l). 20 cm³ of ethene burns in excess oxygen. What volume of carbon dioxide is produced, measured at room temperature and pressure?

options.text: 80 cm³ of carbon dioxide
20 cm³ of the CO2 gas
60 cm³ of CO2 produced
40 cm³ of CO2 formed

items.why: C2H4 : CO2 is 1 : 2 among the gases, so 20 × 2 = 40 cm³ of carbon dioxide.
